meaning.evidence: Every ingredient, step and tip is kept, line for line: "Let stand for about 1 minute and remove from hot baking tray to cool on a wire rack."

sense.evidence: Local swaps carry their sense ("plain flour", "bicarb soda", "baking paper", "wholemeal flour"), but "Use cake flour instead of all-purpose" leaves the US term after the list renamed it, and the tray is called both "baking tray" and "a greased sheet".

authenticity.evidence: Mechanical: the word for the cookie flips between "bickies", "bikkie dough", "biscuit texture" and "bickie", which no Australian writer would do in one recipe; "except choccy and nuts" sits in otherwise formal prose.

register.evidence: Mostly the original's formal recipe English with word swaps ("marg", "choccy", "heaps"); lighter than level 3. No swearing, within vulgarity 1.

tone.evidence: The plain instructional tone is kept: "Add eggs one at a time, beating until fully incorporated."

flow.evidence: Readable, but the shifting nouns jar: "More brown sugar will result in chewier bickies. More white sugar will result in crisper biscuits."

variety.evidence: The variety is random rather than deliberate: "bickies", "bikkies", "biscuits" alternate, and "choccy" is dropped in where "chocolate" stays elsewhere.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the original recipe, structure and notes intact: "Stir in chocolate morsels (chips), and nuts if using."

problems.quote: More brown sugar will result in chewier bickies. More white sugar will result in crisper biscuits.
problems.original: More brown sugar will result in chewier cookies. More white sugar will result in crisper cookies.
problems.why: Inconsistent spellings and words for the same cookie read as machine output.

problems.quote: Use cake flour instead of all-purpose
problems.original: Use cake flour instead of all-purpose
problems.why: US "all-purpose" left after the ingredient list switched to "plain flour".

problems.quote: 5 oz (150 g) chopped nuts, such as groundnuts (optional)
problems.original: 5 oz (150 g) chopped nuts, such as groundnuts (optional)
problems.why: "groundnuts" left where "peanuts" is the local word.

A.summary: Complete but mechanical; the cookie's name keeps changing and much stays formal.

meaning.evidence: Everything is kept: "Let them sit for about 1 minute, then take them off the hot baking tray to cool on a wire rack." Nothing added.

sense.evidence: Every swap fits: "plain flour", "bicarb soda", "choc bits", "peanuts", "baking paper", "rolled oats", "chopped-up block chocolate".

authenticity.evidence: Reads like an Australian recipe: "you mightn't like it in the bikkies either", "bump the flour up to 3+ cups", "won't cool as quick".

register.evidence: A light, conversational level 3 suited to a recipe ("Some people also reckon", "won't spread heaps"); perhaps a touch light. No swearing.

tone.evidence: Keeps the plain, helpful instructional tone: "If you beat it too long, you can get some gluten forming, which will change the bikkie texture."

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "There should be enough fat in the bikkie dough to stop it sticking, but baking paper or non-stick trays may help if you find it does stick."

variety.evidence: "bikkies" is the cookie throughout, which is consistent; otherwise the slang is light and not leaned on ("reckon", "heaps", "bump the flour up").

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original recipe, with its notes in order: "Do not stack" becomes "Don't stack hot bikkies or they'll bend out of shape".

problems.quote: Some people also reckon you should chill the dough before baking
problems.original: Some people also recommend chilling dough before baking
problems.why: Fine, but the slang overall is thin for level 3.

B.summary: A clean, natural Australian recipe; a little light on slang.

meaning.evidence: All steps and notes kept. "dark choc bits" for semi-sweet chocolate is the local equivalent, and "swap two teaspoons of the white sugar for vanilla sugar" keeps the substitution.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "not much chop to eat on its own", "Top-shelf butter", "Chuck in the vanilla", "On the flip side". "a cracker of a bikkie" fits "a superior cookie".

authenticity.evidence: Natural and local: "Get the oven heating", "pop them in the 350°F oven", "if you reckon the chocolate's too bitter".

register.evidence: Right on level 3 for a recipe: a steady sprinkle ("Chuck in", "not much chop", "bump up the spread", "Top-shelf") without turning it into a yarn. No swearing.

tone.evidence: Instructional tone kept, friendly but clear: "just make sure the bits are small enough to eat comfortably."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "If you beat this too long, you might get some gluten forming, which'll change the texture of your bikkies."

variety.evidence: Well varied: "Chuck in", "bump up", "tweak", "cut down", "On the flip side", "cracker", "pop them in".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original, retold: "Using cake flour and brown sugar means you can use butter without worrying about your bikkies turning into puddles".

problems.quote: Top-shelf butter, chocolate and vanilla will make a cracker of a bikkie.
problems.original: Using top-quality butter, chocolate, and vanilla will produce a superior cookie.
problems.why: "Top-shelf" usually describes liquor; fine but slightly odd for butter.

C.summary: Natural, well-pitched and faithful; one of the best.

meaning.evidence: All points survive, but some are changed or added: "your bikkies turn out tough as old boots" for "change the cookie texture", "peanuts or whatever's in the cupboard", "cream the lot till it's all pale and fluffy", and "Careful, the tray's bloody hot."

sense.evidence: Most terms fit ("Give cake flour a burl", "not much chop", "no matter how flash it is"), but "a better bit of chew to 'em" narrows "mouth-feel".

authenticity.evidence: Very natural Australian voice: "Can't get your mitts on vanilla extract?", "Rubbish in, rubbish out." A couple of lines feel tacked on: "Okay, so.", "No judgement."

register.evidence: Heavier than level 3, with a chatty persona and asides ("No judgement.", "Simple as.", "Rubbish in, rubbish out.") and one "bloody", within vulgarity 1.

tone.evidence: The recipe stays a recipe, but the jokey persona tips it towards banter: "if you're a chewy bikkie person. No judgement."

flow.evidence: Lively but choppy, with fragment tags: "More brown sugar, chewier bikkies. More white sugar, crisper ones. Simple as."

variety.evidence: Varied slang ("burl", "mitts", "Bung in", "Muck about"), but tag lines repeat: "Cooling rack, every time", "Nice soft middle, every time."

essence.evidence: Still the original recipe, but the added persona shifts its character: "Okay, so. First up, crank the oven".

problems.quote: Beat the daylights out of it and you'll get gluten forming, and then your bikkies turn out tough as old boots.
problems.original: If you beat this too long, you may get some gluten formation which will change the cookie texture.
problems.why: States a specific result the original leaves general.
Added warning; colour off the hot tray but adds a swear the recipe didn't need.

problems.quote: peanuts or whatever's in the cupboard
Okay, so. First up, crank the oven
problems.why: Persona opener and tags ("No judgement.") push past the brief.

D.summary: Vivid and natural but heavier than asked, with small changes to the instructions.

meaning.evidence: Every step and tip survives; "every oven's a bit different" for "cooking times may vary". Only "peanuts or whatever" loosens the original.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "Don't go overboard beating it", "not stress about your bikkies going all puddly", "not much chop", "no matter how flash it is", "Bung in more vanilla extract".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Australian home cook: "Chuck the eggs in one at a time", "baking paper or non-stick trays'll sort you out", "You can muck about with the mix".

register.evidence: Level 3 throughout: regular, natural slang without asides or persona. No swearing.

tone.evidence: Friendly but still instructional: "just make sure the bits are small enough to eat comfortably."

flow.evidence: Reads like it was written that way: "Tip them into the wet mix in two goes and fold till it's all come together."

variety.evidence: Varied: "crank", "Chuck", "Plonk", "Bung in", "Throw in", "muck about", "sort you out".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original recipe, retold: "which is the only reason anyone uses marg in the first place".

problems.quote: 5 oz (150 g) chopped nuts, peanuts or whatever (optional)
problems.original: 5 oz (150 g) chopped nuts, such as groundnuts (optional)

E.summary: Natural, varied and faithful level 3; the best of the set.
